solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Appeal of strange archaism (8)

indicatorNotes.strange: strange letters are out of their usual order

annotation.surface: Someone finds an old-fashioned turn of phrase oddly attractive.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole anagram is one word, and 'archaism' uses exactly the letters of CHARISMA, which is easy to miss because the two words look nothing alike.
annotation.definitionFit: Charisma is personal appeal, the quality that draws people to someone.

entries.clue: Element serene as clique on regular basis is accommodated (7)

indicatorNotes.on regular basis: take letters at regular intervals, every other one
indicatorNotes.is accommodated: the letters are housed inside another word

blocks.note: the odd letters of CLIQUE: C, I, U

annotation.surface: A calm person is welcomed into an exclusive group on a regular basis.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On regular basis' sounds like how often the clique meets, but it tells you to take every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A category definition: the metal in bones and chalk is one of the chemical elements.

entries.clue: With change of heart, put one’s name forward in suitable way (5)

indicatorNotes.With change of heart: the heart is the middle letter, and it is swapped for another

blocks.note: to apply is to put your name forward, for a job say
the middle P of APPLY becomes T

annotation.surface: Someone changes their mind and then puts themselves forward in the right way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' reads as a change of mind, but here the heart is the middle letter of APPLY. The clue does not say what the new letter is; the definition supplies it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the adverb: fittingly, appropriately, in a suitable manner.

entries.clue: Unfriendly lip, one’s habit unfortunately (12)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: the letters have ended up badly placed, so rearrange them

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters; one’s is read as ONES

annotation.surface: Someone complains that another person's habit of giving lip is unfriendly.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'one’s' is ignored, so it contributes the four letters ONES. 'Lip' here is cheek or insolence, which keeps the surface sounding like a complaint.
annotation.definitionFit: Inhospitable means unwelcoming or unfriendly to guests or strangers.

entries.clue: Stone worker’s two family members (5)

blocks.note: ma = mother, the first of the two
a son, the second of the two

annotation.surface: A stonemason's business employs two of his relatives.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Two family members' is one phrase that yields two pieces, mother and son. The apostrophe-s is 'has', joining the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A mason is a builder or carver who works in stone.

entries.clue: Crossword feature, everything ultimately clear? (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: at the end, so take the last letter

blocks.note: to rid is to clear, as in rid the house of mice

annotation.surface: A solver wonders whether the crossword is finally all sorted out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Everything ultimately clear?' reads as asking whether it all makes sense in the end, but 'ultimately' only picks out the G.
annotation.definitionFit: The grid is the pattern of squares every crossword is built on.

entries.clue: Showing dependence, payment containing pounds I advanced (7)

indicatorNotes.containing: the payment holds the other letters inside it

blocks.note: rent is a regular payment for a home
L = pounds, from the Latin libra
A = advanced, as in A level

annotation.surface: Someone depends on a payment that includes money they lent out earlier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I advanced' sounds like a loan, but it is two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: To be reliant is to depend on someone or something.

entries.clue: Classic hat (5)

blocks.note: the Classics are the five great English flat horse races; this one is run at Epsom
the American name for a bowler, a hard round felt hat

annotation.surface: A timeless style of hat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Classic' looks like an adjective describing the hat, but it is a noun: the Classics are five famous English horse races, and the Derby, run at Epsom, is one.
annotation.definitionFit: The Derby is a Classic race, and a derby is a round hard felt hat.

entries.clue: Delay in mail, quiet — one intended, they say (12)

indicatorNotes.they say: what people say is heard, so go by sound

blocks.note: meant = intended; MENT is said the same way

annotation.surface: A late letter, and someone quietly explains that one was meant to arrive.
annotation.walkthrough: Only 'intended' is heard rather than read: MEANT becomes the ending MENT.
annotation.definitionFit: A postponement is a delay, putting something off to a later time.

entries.clue: Learner at church door might have this (5)

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L plates on a learner driver's car
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

annotation.surface: A novice waits at the church door.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition runs on from the wordplay: 'church door' looks like one thing, but 'church' ends the wordplay and 'door might have this' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A latch is the simple catch that holds a door or gate shut.

entries.clue: Untimely disclosure in peril — so disorganised (7)

indicatorNotes.disorganised: the letters are out of order

annotation.surface: A secret leaked too early puts a badly run operation in danger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Untimely disclosure' sounds like a political leak, but it is the modern sense: someone giving away the ending of a film or book.
annotation.definitionFit: A spoiler reveals a plot twist or ending before you've seen it, a disclosure at the wrong time.

entries.clue: Climbing plant of creamy white colour, not gold (3)

indicatorNotes.not: the colour without the gold, so remove it

blocks.note: OR = gold in heraldry; take it out of IVORY

annotation.surface: A climbing plant with cream-coloured flowers, without any golden ones.
annotation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold, a convention worth learning.
annotation.definitionFit: Ivy is an evergreen plant that climbs walls and trees.

entries.clue: Refuge in Tuscany a builder finally revamped (9)

indicatorNotes.finally: the last letter of the word before
indicatorNotes.revamped: done up anew, so rearrange the letters

annotation.surface: A builder restores an old place in Tuscany to make a retreat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revamped' fits the builder so well it hides that it acts on the letters. Tuscany is the region of Italy around Florence.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a place people flee to for protection, as churches once were for fugitives.

entries.clue: One seen as different if making a comeback in film (6)

indicatorNotes.making a comeback: coming back, so write the word the other way round
indicatorNotes.in: put the letters inside the next word

blocks.note: a film is a thin layer, like a mist on glass

annotation.surface: An actor who stood out as unusual may be returning to the movies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Film' reads as a movie, which suits a comeback, but it means a thin haze.
annotation.definitionFit: A misfit is someone who does not fit in, seen as different from those around them.

entries.clue: Outside expert on navigating the web? (7)

blocks.note: to surf the web is to browse from page to page
ace = expert; 'on' ties the expert to the activity, so it follows the web word

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a person who knows the internet is really an outsider.
annotation.walkthrough: The pieces sit in the order of the phrase 'surf ace', an expert at surfing, rather than the order of the clue. The question mark flags that playful reading.
annotation.definitionFit: The surface is the outside or outer layer of something.

entries.clue: Confused store with right list (6)

indicatorNotes.Confused: a confused mind has its thoughts jumbled, so the letters come out jumbled too

annotation.surface: A muddled shop has the correct inventory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right' joins STORE before the letters are mixed, so all six go into the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A roster is a list, especially of people and their duties.

entries.clue: Compensation as daughter becomes good — move back (7)

annotation.surface: A daughter gets compensation and turns good, then relapses.
annotation.walkthrough: Swap the D of REDRESS for G. Only the first D changes; the other letters stay put.
annotation.definitionFit: To regress is to go back to an earlier, often worse, state.

entries.clue: Made to conceal weapon, article left something applied to soldier? (9)

indicatorNotes.to conceal: the outer word hides the others inside it

annotation.surface: Someone forced to hide a gun gets something smeared on a soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a soldier is also a finger of toast for dipping, which is what the marmalade goes on; the question mark flags it.
annotation.definitionFit: Marmalade is a citrus preserve spread on toast, including toast cut into soldiers.

entries.clue: It’s nice to hear Manchester United survive in Cup initially (5)

annotation.definitionNote: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so take first letters

blocks.clueFragment: Manchester United survive in Cup initially
blocks.note: first letters of Manchester, United, Survive, In, Cup

annotation.surface: A football fan is glad to hear that Manchester United are still in the Cup.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a description rather than a synonym, and the question of whether United survive makes 'music to my ears' fit the surface too.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition, not a synonym: organised sound people enjoy listening to, as in 'music to my ears'.

entries.clue: Clinical pharmacy shows character (5)

indicatorNotes.shows: the words display the answer within them

annotation.surface: A hospital pharmacy reveals what kind of place it is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as personality, but it is a letter of an alphabet: alpha is the first Greek letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Alpha is a character, the first letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Interest in British silver (3)

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

annotation.surface: Someone takes an interest in British silverware.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Interest' is in the informal sense: something that is your bag is your thing, what you're into.
annotation.definitionFit: Your bag is the thing you're interested in or good at.

entries.clue: It’s next after 18! Well done! (5)

blocks.note: 18 down's answer opens the NATO phonetic alphabet; the code word after it is wanted

annotation.surface: Someone cheers reaching the next number after eighteen.
annotation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 18 down, ALPHA, so you need that answer first. 'After 18' looks like a matter of age or numbers.
annotation.definitionFit: Bravo follows Alpha in the phonetic alphabet, and 'bravo!' is a shout of well done.

entries.clue: Concession about name for shellfish (7)

indicatorNotes.about: around, so the concession goes around the name

blocks.note: a sop is a small concession to keep someone quiet

annotation.surface: Someone gives ground on what to call a type of shellfish.
annotation.walkthrough: CALL goes inside SO…P. 'About' looks like 'concerning' but is here 'around'.
annotation.definitionFit: A scallop is an edible shellfish with a fan-shaped ribbed shell.

entries.clue: Strike out and render a service to some extent (5)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: only part of the words is used

annotation.surface: A worker goes on strike yet still offers partial help.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strike out' sounds like industrial action or a baseball out, but it means deleting text.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: crossing a word out and rubbing it away both remove it from the page.

entries.clue: Maybe rowers boasted (4)

blocks.note: the team of rowers in a boat; 'maybe' marks rowers as one example
an old past tense of crow, meaning to boast

annotation.surface: Rowers who may have bragged about their race.
annotation.walkthrough: CREW as the past of crow (boast) is rare but still in dictionaries; crowed is the usual form.
annotation.definitionFit: A crew can be a team of rowers, and crew is a past tense of crow, to boast.

entries.clue: Wary, promises to pay after share-out, with first part of addition included (8)

indicatorNotes.after: the IOUs come after the other piece
indicatorNotes.first part of: the first part of a word is its opening letter, here the A of addition

blocks.note: a cut is a share of the takings
IOUs are written promises to pay a debt

annotation.surface: Someone is wary of IOUs after a share-out when extra charges have been added.
annotation.walkthrough: A goes inside CU…T, then IOUS follows. 'Share-out' is a division of money, one's cut.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe holding back for fear of danger or being caught out.
